1.pericope_label: By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up my love

schools.summary: Reads the episode as a dream and uses that to dissolve its difficulties, since in a dream imagination outruns reflection; and treats the whole as a poet's reminiscence of love before the marriage rather than as record or allegory.
Takes the night for the darkness of the Old Testament church under the ceremonial shadow, and reads the plural nights as constancy in seeking rather than as recurring doubt.
Divides between a literal eastern wedding, dated to its third night, and a thoroughgoing allegory of Christ sought and withdrawn, with the watchmen as ministers and the mother as the church above.
Sets the failure of the search down to the seeker, calling it late and lazy, and gives the allegory a history in the long waiting of the Old Testament church.

debates.question: What kind of thing is this passage?

positions.view: allegory: the night is the darkness of the Old Testament church under the ceremonial shadow, and Christ's absence makes night as his presence makes day
allegory with a history: it was hard for that church to find Christ in the types and figures, and the consolation of Israel was long looked for before an old man held him at last
a literal eastern wedding: the bridegroom came only by night, and on this night did not come as usual
a poem: a reminiscence of the intensity of their love before their union, put by the poet into his lady's mouth
a dream: on any outward account her question to the watchmen would be foolish, but in a dream feeling and imagination rise higher than reflection

debates.question: Why did the first search fail?

positions.view: because the seeking was late and lazy, the understanding clouded and the affections chilled, as with the virgins who slumbered in the bridegroom's absence
either because she had not sought him diligently or because she had abused his favour; the choice is left open
because she had taken a wrong method, and had to leave her bed of sloth before she could find him
because the sense of being forgotten returned night after night until she grew distrustful of his fidelity, her longing growing as her fear grew

outliers.reading: Alone notices that she never names the man she is looking for, thinking it needless that anyone in such an office could fail to know him, and that the watchmen's answer goes unrecorded either because it was no answer or because their silence told her they could not help.

Alone illustrates the watchmen from a modern traveller's account of an eastern city after dark, where the streets are deserted and the guard creeps about and arrests anyone found walking without a light.

themes: By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?

It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me.
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.

6.pericope_label: Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness: behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him

schools.summary: Defines the wilderness as open nomad country rather than a spiritual condition, argues the etymology of the untranslatable word through four languages, and distinguishes the court women from the city at large.
Reads the wilderness as the state of nature before conversion, the bed as the visible church, and the silver pillars as the doctrines of the gospel.

Divides again between the literal wedding, with its incense and its plated bedposts, and an allegory in which the vehicle is the word of Christ and the incorruptible cedar the word that endures for ever.

Counts the occurrences of the royal name and builds on its meaning of peace, distinguishing those who merely dwell at ease from those who dwell in safety, and reads the coming up from the wilderness three ways at once.

debates.question: What is the vehicle the king made, a word occurring nowhere else?

positions.view: a palanquin or litter, on two grounds: the context describes the approach of a royal procession, and the word rendered covering suits a movable litter rather than a bed of state
very likely a nuptial bed rather than a chariot, though it may be a palanquin

any of several things: a bride chamber, a portable nuptial bed, the open chariot that carried a bride from her father's house, an ancient litter like a sedan, or the vehicle in which bride, bridegroom and friend rode together
the word of Christ dispensed by his ministers, in which he rides triumphantly and believers are carried to glory

debates.question: What is the wilderness she comes up from?

positions.view: open country, the land of nomads as distinguished from that of a settled population
the state of nature before conversion, barren and full of perplexing tracks
the Gentile world out of which believers are called, the pillars of smoke recalling the cloud that led Israel
three things at once: the nation coming up after forty years of wandering, any public deliverance of the church, and the recovery of a single soul out of desertion

outliers.reading: Alone makes the royal pageant a foil rather than the subject, taking the scene as passing in the theatre of the fancy and introduced to set the simplicity of the poet's own espousals, where the joy centred wholly in true love, against the pomp of a state marriage.

Alone counts the occurrences of the name Solomon, three here and three in all the rest of the song, and builds on its meaning peace the distinction that those who rest in Christ not only dwell at ease, as many do who are in great danger, but dwell in safety.

themes: Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?
Behold his bed, which is Solomon’s; threescore valiant men are about it, of the valiant of Israel.
They all hold swords, being expert in war: every man hath his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night.
King Solomon made himself a chariot of the wood of Lebanon.
He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.
Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the gladness of his heart.
